text2.1: In truth, brown bears are timid and highly strung. They do not normally attack people; when they see a human, they flee.
text3.1: In recent years, however, changes in forest environments and in human society have increased the friction between bears and people.
text3.2: Friction (atsureki) … a state of conflict and hostility between humans and brown bears.
text4.1: Bears do not come down to inhabited areas in order to attack people. They act to adapt to the environment they now face, and as a result some become problem animals and are culled.
text5.1: What we — the young people of Hokkaido — can do to reduce the friction with brown bears.
text7.1:
It is to take ownership of the issue between bears and people, and to learn how brown bears really live.
Let this be your chance to get to know the brown bear, the symbol of Hokkaido's magnificent wild nature.
bento_intro.1:
Do you know how much a brown bear weighs, how tall it stands, or what it eats?
Let's start with the basics.
kotaigun.2: Hokkaido is a large island, and even within a single species, population density, geography and the relationship with people differ from region to region. The bears are therefore divided into five local populations.
kotaigun.5: Terrain: a narrow peninsula where steep mountains run down close to the coast
kotaigun.6: Friction: mountains and residential areas lie close together, so people and bears are also close.
kotaigun.9: Terrain: found in the area between the Kuromatsunai Lowland, where Oshamambe lies, and the Ishikari Lowland, where Sapporo lies.
kotaigun.10: Friction: as numbers have grown and the range expanded in recent years, friction with people has become serious in built-up areas such as Sapporo.
kotaigun.13: Terrain: distributed mainly across the Hidaka and Yubari mountain ranges
kotaigun.14: Friction: crop damage has long been common along the foot of the mountains
kotaigun.17: Terrain: distributed across the Teshio and Mashike mountains
kotaigun.18: Friction: numbers once fell sharply, but in recent years they have turned upward and the range is expanding. Crop damage has risen steeply of late.
kotaigun.21: Terrain: distributed across an area taking in the Daisetsuzan range, the Shiretoko Peninsula and the Shiranuka Hills
kotaigun.22: Friction: large-scale dairy and arable farmland surrounds the forest, so crop damage along the boundary has been frequent for many years.
kisetsunotabemono.2: Brown bears belong to the order Carnivora, but they are in fact omnivores. What they eat varies with region and environment, though plant matter naturally makes up the greater part of their diet.
kisetsunotabemono.3: Because the plants available change through the year, their diet differs greatly from season to season.
kisetsunotabemono.5: They eat mainly herbaceous plants such as butterbur, skunk cabbage, Asian skunk cabbage and members of the carrot family. They also feed on the carcasses of sika deer that did not survive the winter, and sometimes prey on slow-moving fawns.
kisetsunotabemono.7: They still eat herbaceous plants such as butterbur and members of the carrot family, but feed mainly on insects and crustaceans such as ants, wasps and crayfish, and on fruit such as raspberries and mulberries.
kisetsunotabemono.8: The turn from summer to autumn is the season when herbaceous plants have grown tough and the nuts have not yet ripened. Food is therefore easily in short supply at this time.
kisetsunotabemono.10: They feed mainly on nuts such as acorns and walnuts, and on soft fruits such as wild grapes and hardy kiwi. They take in a great many calories to build up fat for hibernation.
taijuu.2: The brown bear is the largest land animal in Japan.
taijuu.3: Males usually top out in the 300 kg range, but individuals approaching 500 kg have been recorded in the past.
taijuu.5: Brown bears hibernate, taking neither food nor water and passing no waste through the winter. Come autumn they therefore eat large quantities of acorns, hardy kiwi and the like, laying down subcutaneous fat for hibernation. Their weight falls from spring through summer and rises sharply in autumn. Because they live off the stored fat during winter, they are much lighter again by spring.
taijuu.7: The higher the proportion of meat in the diet — fish such as salmon, or the flesh of other animals — the larger bears in that region tend to grow.
shincho.2: Brown bears sometimes rise onto their hind legs to scan their surroundings or to threaten. A bear standing upright is as tall as a person, or taller.
shincho.4: Adults grow to this size, yet a newborn cub, born inside the den during hibernation, is only some 20–30 cm long and weighs about 400 g. From a size that fits in a human palm, in two to three years it grows to 130–160 cm and 70–120 kg (for a male).
shincho.5: It takes years to reach full size
shincho.6: People have their growth spurt, and bears too need a considerable time to reach their full length. Females generally stop growing at around four to six years old, but males keep growing slowly for several more years, until about eight to ten. An exceptionally large male is therefore almost always a seasoned old bear that has survived many years in a harsh natural world.
koudohani.2: Each brown bear has its own established home range.
koudohani.3: Home ranges cover several hundred square kilometres for males and several tens for females, so males range more widely than females. Males roam in search of mates for breeding, which is why their range is larger. Range size also varies with the region and the amount of food available, and is smaller where food is plentiful. Brown bears hold no territory in the sense of an area from which others are excluded, and their home ranges overlap with those of other bears.
ichinichinokodo.2: Brown bears living in the mountains are basically diurnal, and are relatively active in the early morning and evening. Like people, they are active by day and sleep at night. Near inhabited areas, however, they often stay hidden and move about at night so as not to be seen.
ichinichinokodo.5: Back rubbing covers behaviours such as stripping bark, biting and rubbing the body against a tree. It becomes active during the May–July breeding season and peaks in June. The purpose is thought to be communication between individuals, and males use it especially often. Thick conifers such as Sakhalin fir along game trails and forest roads are selected for the purpose.
ichinichinokodo.7: When a brown bear obtains food too large to finish at once, such as a deer carcass, it covers it with soil, branches and whatever else lies around to hide it, and stays nearby for a while. This is known as a domanjū, or earth mound. Approach one and the bear may attack to defend its food. A bear may be lying in wait near a deer carcass, so never go near one.
kotaisu.2: The estimated brown bear population of Hokkaido was about 11,661.
kotaisu.3: Compared with the 5,800 ± 2,300 estimated in 1990, the population has doubled in roughly 30 years. It rose steadily from the 1990s through 2022, with a slight decline in 2023 reflecting an increase in culling.
kalorie.2: A brown bear eats about 20,000 calories a day
kalorie.3: How much a bear eats varies greatly with age, sex and build. An adult male gets through some 13 kg of food a day, spread over several meals. Seasonal variation is marked, and intake is especially large in autumn, ahead of the winter den.
kalorie.4: Putting an adult male's daily intake (13 kg) in terms of human food…
kalorie.8: The brown bears at Maruyama Zoo in Sapporo
kalorie.9: Their usual daily pattern is said to be a large amount in the morning and at midday, with a lighter meal in the evening. The difference between the sexes is also large: females eat around 10–15 kg a day, while males can put away as much as 24 kg.
kisetsubetsukodo.2: Just after the thaw <emerging from the den>
kisetsubetsukodo.3: The brown bear's eyes and ears are small, but its nose juts out long in front. Its sense of smell is highly developed — said to be six times keener than a dog's. It can pick up the scent of food hundreds of metres away, or buried in the ground. The brown bear lives by its nose.
kisetsubetsukodo.5: Males roam over a wide area in search of females. To pass on their own line, adult males have a habit of killing cubs they have not fathered. Mother bears with cubs may therefore avoid forested mountain areas in order to protect them.
kisetsubetsukodo.7: This is the gap between the period when bears live mainly on herbaceous plants and the period when they turn to nuts, and food in the forest grows scarce. Salmon begin running up the rivers from this time, but the areas where they do so — the Shiretoko Peninsula and a few others — are very limited. Because bears shift their range in search of food, this is when they are most likely to be seen. Farmland holds an abundance of highly nutritious crops, making this the worst season of the year for crop damage.
kisetsubetsukodo.9: Bears eat a great deal to build up reserves for hibernation. Nuts such as acorns and walnuts normally crop abundantly, so food is not usually a problem; but in a poor year the bears widen their range and travel far.
kisetsubetsukodo.11: Once they have built up sufficient reserves, brown bears hibernate in a den. Dens fall into two types: those dug in under the roots of a tree, and earth dens dug straight into the ground. Those that make use of natural cavities can be divided further into rock caves and hollow trees. Pregnant females give birth during hibernation and raise their cubs in the den until spring.
gokan.3: The brown bear's eyes and ears are small, but its nose juts out long in front. Its sense of smell is highly developed — said to be six times keener than a dog's. It can pick up the scent of food hundreds of metres away, or buried in the ground. The brown bear lives by its nose.
gokan.5: Their hearing is excellent and they are highly sensitive to sound. Brown bears are known to be strongly wary of low-frequency sound of around 80–120 Hz, and of sudden loud noises of around 130 dB. They also react sensitively to human footsteps and voices, and will often leave the area when they sense people nearby.
gokan.7: A brown bear's eyesight is considered poorer than a human's and it is weak on distant stationary objects, but it has good night vision and is sensitive to movement. Weaker though it is than smell and hearing, it allows the bear to be active from day into night — and since bears are most active at dawn and dusk, care is needed then.
gokan.9: As well as acorns and skunk cabbage, they find wild vegetables, fruit and farm crops as tasty as we do. They have large canines, but because their food is mainly plant matter their molars are shaped for grinding.
gokan.11: What matters most in a brown bear's sense of touch are the vibrissae — the whiskers around the mouth and eyes. These act as sensors for reading the surroundings in darkness or thick undergrowth. Through their sensitive nose and the soles of their feet they also detect faint vibrations from prey and terrain.
text10.1: Hokkaido, the largest prefecture in Japan.
text11.1:
Brown bears live scattered thinly across a vast wilderness —
isn't that the image you have?
text12.1: In global terms, however, this is a region where bears and people live together at remarkably high density.
text12.2: Brown bear habitat worldwide has a human population density of roughly 0–2 people per km². In Hokkaido it is 69 per km².
text13.1: In other words, in Hokkaido bears and people are inseparably bound together.
text14.1: Let's look at what is actually happening.
q1.1: There's a lot of news lately about bears appearing in residential areas. Why?
a1.1: A: It is not something as simple as numbers rising and bears running out of places to live — several factors combine.
a1.2: Late summer is naturally a season when food is short, so bears widen their search and are more likely to turn up in built-up areas.
a1.3: The bears most likely to appear are females that have gradually settled in over time, and young bears that stray into town while travelling far in search of independence.
a1.4: Human-derived attractants — kitchen waste, compost bins, out-of-spec produce dumped in fields — have taught bears that these are rewarding places, and that too is a factor.
a1.5: Orchards and farmland near forests hold plenty of food a bear can use.
q2.1: Why do bears turn up in farmland again and again?
a2.1: A: With food scarce in the forest and sika deer numbers rising sharply, brown bears have come to depend on farm crops.
a2.2: Farmland margins have become an "attractive sink", setting up a vicious cycle in which new bears flow in from the interior to fill the space left by each cull.
a2.3: It has also been pointed out that indiscriminate culling with box traps prevents bears from learning what is dangerous, and may draw still more of them in.
a2.4: Fewer farmers and large-scale mechanisation have thinned out the human presence, weakening the area's defences — another reason the visits keep recurring.
q3.1: Sika deer numbers are rising. How does that relate to brown bears?
a3.1: A: As sika deer have increased, so has the share of deer in the brown bear's diet.
a3.2: The rise in the sika deer population and the share of newborn fawns taken by brown bears move in proportion.
a3.3: Deer exclusion fences and increased hunting have left more deer carcasses about, which also affects what bears eat.
a3.4: It has been suggested that the increase in sika deer may have raised brown bear survival, reproduction and growth rates.
a3.5: Grazing by sika deer and other herbivores has reduced the biomass of forest-floor vegetation and changed its species composition, contributing to the shortage of food for bears in the forest.
measure_tools.1: What to carry when going near bear country
measure_tools.3: To avoid becoming a victim, the first essential is to let bears know we are there.
measure_tools.4: It is also worth carrying something that can drive a bear off, in case the worst happens and one comes close.
measure_tools.5: Click the items on the left to see how each one is used.
measure_garbage.1: Follow the rules for putting out rubbish
measure_garbage.2: Bears have a keen sense of smell, and once they learn the taste of rubbish they return to the same spot again and again. Putting rubbish out correctly reduces bear visits and keeps the area safe.
measure_garbage.4: Always seal rubbish in a bag or container so no smell escapes. This also stops bears learning where the rubbish is.
measure_garbage.6: Do not leave crop waste from households or farms lying about; dispose of it properly.
measure_garbage.7: Avoid putting rubbish out at night
measure_garbage.8: Bears are active at night, so putting rubbish out after dark raises the risk.
measure_info.1: Keep up with bear sighting information
measure_info.2: There are sources such as the prefectural government site, which collates bear sightings, and Higumap, where anyone can share and post sightings and signs.
measure_info.3: Before heading out, check the information from your municipality and local police as well, and stay out of dangerous areas. If you find a bear or signs of one, please help by reporting it to Higumap or a similar service.
coexistence.1: Towards coexistence with brown bears in Hokkaido
coexistence.2: On a single island, brown bears and people each seek a different environment. Both have a large influence on the ecosystem — so what is needed for them to coexist over the long term?
coexistence.3: It is essential to advance research on brown bears and to build a management system that achieves both conservation of the species and the removal of problem animals. On that foundation, we need to work in parallel on an environment that denies bears access to human food, and on restoring natural habitat in which they can live without it.
coexistence.4: In 2022 Hokkaido published the Hokkaido Brown Bear Management Plan (Phase 2). Its aim is to secure the survival of the local populations while making flexible use of the latest technology such as ICT and of scientific knowledge, and to further strengthen comprehensive measures for reducing friction — from preventing bear visits to responding when they occur.
coexistence.5: In 2025 the Japanese government announced its Bear Damage Countermeasures Package. This responds to a grave situation in which deaths caused by bears have reached a record high and injuries are growing, diversifying and spreading over wider areas. To protect people's lives and livelihoods, the relevant ministries and agencies are working together to roll out effective measures in stages.
coexistence.6: Through these efforts, the national government and Hokkaido aim to achieve both conservation of the brown bear and minimisation of the harm it causes.

tool_bell.2: A tool for defending yourself when a brown bear attacks, by spraying it at the bear. In North America it has stopped bear attacks more than 90% of the time.
tool_bell.3: The active ingredient is mainly capsaicin (chilli extract). It gives an intense irritation to the bear's eyes, nose and the mucous membranes of the mouth, temporarily taking away its sight and its breathing so that you can escape.
tool_spray.2: A tool for defending yourself when a brown bear attacks, by spraying it at the bear. In North America it has stopped bear attacks more than 90% of the time.
tool_spray.3: The active ingredient is mainly capsaicin (chilli extract). It gives an intense irritation to the bear's eyes, nose and the mucous membranes of the mouth, temporarily taking away its sight and its breathing so that you can escape.
tool_bearhorn.2: A bear horn uses compressed gas or hand power to produce a piercing high-frequency blast, letting bears know you are there or startling them into moving away.
tool_bearhorn.3: It is effective where sound is easily drowned out, such as on windy days or near a river.
tool_handy_radio.2: Playing human voices and similar sounds puts brown bears on their guard.
tool_handy_radio.3: It helps signal that there are people around.
